title: Greedy Florist
directAnswer: The price of a flower is its original cost times one plus the number of flowers that buyer has ALREADY purchased. To minimise the total, the most expensive flowers must be bought first (multiplier 1) and the cheap ones absorb the higher multipliers. Sort the costs descending; the i-th costliest flower (0-indexed) is bought at multiplier (i / k + 1) where k is the number of friends. O(n log n) from the sort.

remember.pattern: Greedy: assign the smallest multipliers to the largest costs (sort descending, round-robin the multiplier)
remember.formula:
sort c descending
total = 0
for i, cost in enumerate(c):
    total += (i // k + 1) * cost   # k = number of friends
return total
rules: A flower's price = `(previous purchases by that friend + 1) * originalCost`. The +1 means the first flower a friend buys costs full price.
Spread purchases evenly across the k friends: with the costs sorted descending, the i-th flower (0-indexed) gets multiplier `i / k + 1`.
Buy **expensive flowers first** so they get the lowest multiplier — the exchange argument proves this is optimal.
`k` is the number of **friends** (buyers), not the number of flowers. Misreading this swaps the multiplier formula.
Integer division `i / k` in Java is floor division — exactly what the round-robin needs; mirror it with `i // k` in Python.
whenToUse: A per-item cost is scaled by a multiplier that grows with how many items the same actor has already taken
You can distribute items across several actors to keep multipliers low
Minimising a sum of (weight × multiplier) where you control which weight gets which multiplier
The multipliers form a fixed multiset and you only choose the pairing
antiSignals: The multiplier depends on the VALUE bought, not just the count → greedy pairing breaks
Buyers have individual budgets or limits → constrained assignment, not a clean sort
Items interact (buying one changes another's cost) → DP or flow
You must minimise the number of buyers under a price cap → different objective entirely
remember.takeaway: When you pair a fixed set of multipliers with a set of weights to minimise the weighted sum, the rearrangement inequality says: pair the largest weight with the smallest multiplier. Sort descending and round-robin the multipliers — the same move appears in any 'assign costs to growing prices' problem.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you correctly model the price function (multiplier = previous purchases + 1) and then realise the optimal pairing is largest-cost-to-smallest-multiplier, distributed evenly across the k friends.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Sorting ascending (so cheap flowers get the low multipliers and expensive ones get inflated), or confusing k = friends with k = flowers.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the rearrangement / exchange argument: if a cheaper flower were bought before a pricier one by the same friend, swapping them lowers the total, so costliest-first is optimal.

problemStatement:
A group of `k` friends wants to buy `n` flowers from a florist. The original price of the `i`-th flower is `c[i]`.

The florist is greedy: the price a customer pays for a flower is `(1 + x) * c[i]`, where `x` is the number of flowers that **same customer** has **already purchased**. The first flower a customer buys costs `1 * c[i]`, the second `2 * c[i]`, and so on.

Every flower must be bought, and each flower is bought by exactly one of the `k` friends. Return the **minimum total cost** to buy all `n` flowers.
understanding: Each friend pays a multiplier that climbs by 1 with every flower they personally buy: 1×, 2×, 3×, … We assign flowers to friends and choose the order each friend buys them. The multipliers available form a fixed pattern — k flowers at 1×, the next k at 2×, and so on — and we only decide which cost gets which multiplier.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is k the number of friends or the number of flowers?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: k is the number of friends (buyers). The number of flowers is n = c.length. Getting this backwards inverts the multiplier formula.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the multiplier reset per friend or accumulate globally?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Per friend. The multiplier is 1 + (flowers that specific friend has already bought), so spreading purchases across friends keeps multipliers low.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must every flower be purchased?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — all n flowers are bought. We're minimising the cost of buying the whole set, not choosing a subset.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can two friends buy the same flower?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Each flower is bought exactly once by exactly one friend.

examples.explanation: 3 friends, 3 flowers — each friend buys one at multiplier 1: 2 + 5 + 6 = 13.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Try Every Order of Purchase
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to show you see the assignment search, then collapse it with the rearrangement observation.
hints: A solution is an assignment of each flower to a friend plus the order each friend buys their flowers. What does that determine for every flower?

Given any full ordering of all n purchases, the multiplier of a flower is fixed by how many that friend already bought. Try every permutation of the flowers and assign multipliers round-robin across friends.
Score each permutation and keep the minimum total. Correct, but n! permutations make it useless beyond tiny n — use it only to motivate sorting.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are n! orderings of the flowers; scoring each costs O(n). No structure is exploited, so the factorial dominates.
approaches.explanation:
Think of a candidate solution as an ordering of all `n` flowers. If we hand them out round-robin to the `k` friends in that order, the flower at position `i` (0-indexed) is bought at multiplier `i / k + 1`: the first `k` positions are each some friend's first purchase (×1), the next `k` are second purchases (×2), and so on.

**Why permuting the flowers covers all cases.** The multiset of multipliers is fixed once `n` and `k` are known — it's always `k` ones, then `k` twos, and so on. The only freedom we have is *which cost receives which multiplier*. Permuting the flowers and applying the positional multiplier `i / k + 1` enumerates every possible pairing.

**Why it's correct but hopeless.** Every assignment is tried, so the minimum found is the true optimum. But there are `n!` permutations; even `n = 12` is half a billion. The brute force exists only to make the structure visible.

**The structure it reveals.** Look at the multiplier sequence `1,1,…,2,2,…`: it's non-decreasing with position. To minimise `Σ multiplier(i) · cost(i)`, the rearrangement inequality says pair the smallest multipliers with the largest costs. That means: sort the costs descending and read off the positional multipliers. No search needed.
approaches.insight: The multipliers are a sorted (non-decreasing) sequence and we just choose how to pair them with costs. Minimising a sum of paired products with one sequence fixed is exactly the rearrangement inequality — oppositely sort the two sequences.

pitfalls: Factorial blow-up — only feasible for n ≤ ~10; it's a teaching device, not a submission.
Forgetting the multiplier is positional under round-robin, not arbitrary.
Minimising the wrong quantity (e.g. number of friends used) instead of total cost.

approaches.name: Greedy — Sort Descending, Round-Robin the Multiplier (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'buy the most expensive flowers first so they pay the smallest multiplier'.
hints: The multipliers you'll pay are fixed: k flowers at 1×, the next k at 2×, and so on. You only choose which cost takes which multiplier. Which cost should get the smallest multiplier?
Put the biggest costs where the multiplier is smallest. Sort the costs descending so the priciest flower sits at position 0 (multiplier 1).
Sweep the sorted-descending array; the flower at index i pays multiplier i / k + 1. Sum (i / k + 1) · c[i]. One pass after the sort.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting the costs is O(n log n) and dominates; the weighted-sum sweep is O(n) with only scalar accumulators → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Sort the costs in **descending** order. Walk the sorted array; the flower at index `i` (0-indexed) is the `(i / k + 1)`-th flower bought by whichever friend handles it under an even round-robin, so it costs `(i / k + 1) · c[i]`. Sum those products.

**Why costliest-first — the exchange argument.** Suppose an optimal plan buys a cheaper flower with cost `a` at a *lower* multiplier `p` while a pricier flower with cost `b > a` is bought at a *higher* multiplier `q > p` (by anyone). Their combined contribution is `p·a + q·b`. Swap the two flowers' purchase slots: now `b` takes multiplier `p` and `a` takes `q`, contributing `p·b + q·a`. The change is `(p·b + q·a) − (p·a + q·b) = (q − p)(a − b) < 0` because `q > p` and `a < b`. The swap strictly lowers the total, so no optimal plan can put a smaller cost at a smaller multiplier than a larger cost. Hence the largest costs must take the smallest multipliers — exactly what sorting descending achieves.

**Why the multiplier is `i / k + 1`.** Spreading purchases as evenly as possible across `k` friends means the first `k` flowers are each some friend's first purchase (×1), the next `k` are second purchases (×2), and so on. Integer-dividing the 0-based index by `k` and adding 1 reproduces this `1,1,…,2,2,…` staircase. An uneven distribution would only push some flower to a *higher* multiplier than necessary, never lower, so even round-robin is optimal.

**Why k = friends matters.** `k` is the count of buyers, so it's the width of each multiplier 'band'. With more friends the bands are wider, more flowers stay at multiplier 1, and the total drops. Confusing `k` with `n` breaks the band width.
approaches.insight: This is the rearrangement inequality in disguise: with the multiplier sequence fixed and non-decreasing, the minimum weighted sum pairs it oppositely with the costs. Sort costs descending against an ascending multiplier staircase. 'One sequence is forced, sort the other the opposite way' is the reusable kernel.

edgeCases.behavior: Every index i < k, so i/k = 0 and every flower pays multiplier 1 — total is just the plain sum.
Multiplier is i + 1; the single friend buys all flowers, paying 1×,2×,3×,… on the descending order.

pitfalls: Sorting ascending — cheap flowers grab the low multipliers and expensive ones get inflated, maximising instead of minimising.
Using n instead of k as the band width — wrong multipliers throughout.
Off-by-one on the multiplier — it's i/k + 1, not i/k (the first purchase is 1×, never 0×).

commonMistakes: Sorting ascending so the priciest flowers absorb the highest multipliers.
Confusing k = number of friends with k = number of flowers.
Using i/k instead of i/k + 1 for the multiplier (the first purchase is full price, ×1).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting ascending instead of descending
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The largest costs must receive the smallest multipliers. Ascending order does the opposite, inflating the total.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
c.sort()
total = sum((i // k + 1) * cost for i, cost in enumerate(c))
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
c.sort(reverse=True)
total = sum((i // k + 1) * cost for i, cost in enumerate(c))

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one in the multiplier
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A friend's first purchase costs 1×, not 0×. The multiplier is i/k + 1; dropping the +1 makes the first band free.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int multiplier = i / k;
total += multiplier * flowers[i];
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int multiplier = i / k + 1;
total += multiplier * flowers[i];

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Treating k as the flower count
commonMistakesDetailed.why: k is the number of friends and sets the band width. Using n splits everyone into their own band and breaks the round-robin.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
n = len(c)
total = sum((i // n + 1) * cost for i, cost in enumerate(c))
commonMistakesDetailed.good: total = sum((i // k + 1) * cost for i, cost in enumerate(c))

patternNote: Rearrangement-inequality greedy: a fixed, sorted multiplier sequence is paired with item weights to minimise a weighted sum. Sort the weights opposite to the multipliers (descending against an ascending staircase). The same kernel drives any 'assign growing prices to costs' problem.
